title: Trump: Barr asks states to charge protesters with attempts to overthrow the government
description_short: Trump: Barr asks states to charge protesters with attempts to overthrow the government
description_medium: During a 2020 conference call, Attorney General William Barr urged federal prosecutors to consider sedition charges against people arrested during racial-justice protests, according to the supplied timeline. The account describes the suggestion as unusual and says it alarmed some U.S. attorneys on the call. It does not identify the call date or establish that any protester was ultimately charged under the proposed theory.
description_long: The supplied timeline says Attorney General William Barr raised the possibility of sedition charges against people arrested during Black Lives Matter protests in a conference call with federal prosecutors in September 2020. It characterizes the proposal as highly unusual and reports that some U.S. attorneys were alarmed by the suggestion. The account does not give the exact date of the call, name the participants who objected, or document a resulting prosecution under that theory. Sedition is a serious federal offense, so applying it to protest activity would raise questions about the boundary between protected political expression and criminal conduct. The description therefore records the reported prosecutorial guidance and the reaction it drew without implying that protest participation itself constituted sedition or that charges followed. The source connects the episode to the Justice Department under Trump through Barr’s role as attorney general. Its available details concern what Barr reportedly asked prosecutors to consider, not a court finding or a settled legal conclusion about any individual protester.

The supplied account says the department linked the cancellations to a data leak more than five years earlier. That leak exposed information about how wealthy people, including Donald Trump, Elon Musk, and Jeff Bezos, managed their tax obligations. title: Trump Admin plans to sell armed military drones to the United Arab Emirates
description_short: Trump Admin plans to sell armed military drones to the United Arab Emirates
description_medium: In November 2020, the Trump administration notified Congress of a planned arms package for the United Arab Emirates valued at more than $23 billion, including armed drones. Reuters separately reported that the drone portion advanced as a $2.9 billion sale. The larger package and the reported drone deal are distinct figures; the proposal was an arms transfer plan, not evidence here of completed delivery.
description_long: The Trump administration notified Congress in November 2020 of a planned package of military sales to the United Arab Emirates valued at more than $23 billion. The proposed equipment included armed unmanned aircraft. Reuters separately reported that the administration was advancing a $2.9 billion drone sale to the UAE. That reported drone transaction should not be conflated with the total value of the wider package. The timeline says Secretary of State Mike Pompeo oversaw the notification and presents the drones as the first armed-drone export under a reinterpretation of a Cold War-era agreement among 34 participating nations. The available description concerns a proposed transfer and the administration’s policy rationale; it does not establish that all equipment was delivered or describe its later use. The plan raised questions about arms-export controls and the consequences of supplying advanced weapons to a regional partner. Keeping the figures distinct matters: $23 billion refers to the broader package, while Reuters’ $2.9 billion figure concerns the drone sale. The event is therefore recorded as an administration decision to advance a major arms proposal, not as a completed transfer of the entire package.

description_long: Donald Trump spoke in Concord, New Hampshire, on January 19, 2024, during the Republican primary campaign. NBC News reported that he repeatedly substituted Nikki Haley’s name while making claims about Nancy Pelosi and security on January 6. Haley had served as Trump’s U.N. ambassador and was then competing against him for the Republican nomination. title: Trump's $916M Loss Carried Forward 18 Years — Paid Near-Zero Tax Most Years
description_short: Trump's $916M Loss Carried Forward 18 Years — Paid Near-Zero Tax Most Years
description_medium: The New York Times reported in 2016 that Donald Trump’s 1995 tax return declared a loss of about $916 million. Under tax rules, business losses may be carried forward to offset income in later years, and the Times said the amount could have reduced his federal tax bills for up to 18 years. The report did not by itself establish fraud or unlawful avoidance.
description_long: A 1995 federal tax return for Donald Trump showed a declared loss of approximately $916 million, according to tax records reported by The New York Times in 2016. U.S. tax rules permit qualifying business losses to be carried forward and used to offset taxable income in subsequent years. The Times reported that the loss could have allowed Trump to avoid federal income taxes for as many as 18 years. The figure was connected in the supplied account to losses from Atlantic City casinos and other business ventures, but the return alone does not establish that every claimed loss was improper or that tax law was violated. The distinction is important: the story described a large reported loss and its potential tax effect, not a judicial or administrative finding of tax fraud. The episode became a prominent example in debates over how loss provisions affect wealthy taxpayers and the transparency of presidential candidates’ finances. This entry records what the reported return and the Times’ analysis indicated while avoiding a stronger conclusion than those materials support.

Trump sold the property in 2008 to a company controlled by Dmitry Rybolovlev’s family trust for $95 million. The supplied correction says it found no credible support for the claim that Epstein advised Trump.
description_long: Donald Trump won the November 2004 bankruptcy auction for Abe Gosman’s Palm Beach oceanfront property, Maison de l’Amitié, with a bid of $41.35 million. Contemporaneous USA Today reporting listed Jeffrey Epstein as a competing bidder at $36 million, which contradicts the existing claim that Epstein advised Trump on the purchase. In 2008, Trump sold the 6.3-acre property for $95 million to a company controlled by a family trust of Dmitry Rybolovlev, according to the Palm Beach Post. The sale drew later scrutiny, including a Senate inquiry reported by that newspaper. The supplied correction does not establish that the transaction involved money laundering, Deutsche Bank financing, or a $96 million sale price, and this description does not repeat those unsupported claims. The difference between the reported purchase bid and later sale price is notable, but the available sources do not by themselves establish the transaction’s full costs, profit, or purpose. The record is best understood as a high-value property auction and resale with documented competing bids and subsequent scrutiny, rather than as proof of an advisory relationship or criminal conduct.

title: Trump Recognizes Jerusalem as Israeli Capital — 60+ Killed in Protests
description_short: Trump Recognizes Jerusalem as Israeli Capital — 60+ Killed in Protests
description_medium: On December 6, 2017, Trump announced U.S. recognition of Jerusalem as Israel’s capital and directed officials to prepare to move the embassy there. The embassy opened in Jerusalem on May 14, 2018. Reuters reported that Israeli forces killed 58 Palestinian protesters in Gaza that day; later reports put the toll above 60. Those deaths occurred months after the announcement, not all on its date.
description_long: Trump announced on December 6, 2017, that the United States would recognize Jerusalem as Israel’s capital and begin preparations to move the U.S. Embassy from Tel Aviv. The archived White House statement documents the decision. The embassy opened in Jerusalem on May 14, 2018, several months later. Reuters reported that Israeli forces killed 58 Palestinian protesters in Gaza on the opening day; later reporting placed that day’s toll above 60. The timing matters: the reported deaths occurred during protests on May 14, 2018, and should not be described as having happened when Trump made the December announcement. The decision reversed longstanding U.S. practice of deferring recognition of Jerusalem’s status to negotiations and drew international attention because the city is claimed by Israelis and Palestinians. The supplied sources support the policy announcement and the reported casualties on the later embassy-opening date. They do not establish that every death in subsequent protests was caused by the announcement alone. This entry describes the policy shift and the connected, later protest context while keeping those events and dates distinct.

It found no federal income tax payments in 10 of the 15 years examined. The reporting raised questions about his reported business losses, but the figures alone are not a finding of unlawful tax avoidance.
description_long: The New York Times reported in September 2020 that Donald Trump paid $750 in federal income taxes in 2016 and another $750 in 2017. The investigation was based on tax records obtained by the newspaper and found that Trump paid no federal income taxes in 10 of the 15 years it examined. The report described recurring business losses and other deductions that reduced taxable income, and it raised questions about the financial claims behind those filings. Trump disputed the reporting, while the available record did not include his complete returns for public review. The episode became a focal point in debates about tax fairness, financial disclosure, and the tax burdens borne by wealthy individuals. This account keeps the scope tied to the years and records the investigation covered and distinguishes low reported payments from a legal conclusion about tax avoidance.

title: Trump Repeatedly Claims 2024 Election Had Fraud Despite Winning
description_short: Trump Repeatedly Claims 2024 Election Had Fraud Despite Winning
description_medium: After Congress certified his 2024 victory on January 6, 2025, Trump made statements casting doubt on vote counting despite having won the election. The supplied account cites a January 7 press conference and a January 19 rally remark about Pennsylvania vote-counting computers. It does not show that he explicitly alleged those computers changed the result, so that implication should remain qualified.
description_long: Congress certified the 2024 presidential election result on January 6, 2025, confirming Trump’s victory. The supplied account says that at a press conference the next day, Trump remarked that some areas were still counting votes, and that at a January 19 pre-inauguration rally he praised Elon Musk’s knowledge of Pennsylvania vote-counting computers. The same account says Trump later described his win as a “massive mandate,” although his margin was smaller than the popular-vote margin Joe Biden had achieved in 2020. These statements could encourage doubt about the counting process, especially because they followed formal certification of Trump’s own result. The record does not establish that Trump explicitly claimed the computers had manipulated votes or that the remarks changed any election result. It is therefore important to separate the documented comments from interpretations about their intended meaning. The episode is relevant to election confidence because public figures’ descriptions of counting and certification can shape how supporters view legitimate outcomes. The available source and synopsis support an account of post-election rhetoric, not proof of a computer-based conspiracy.
